# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. Looking for "Competence Porn" movies where the characters are locked in

**Score:** 713
**Body:** I'm looking for movies where there's a group of people planning the HECK out of the problem they got themselves into, preferably hard science fiction but I'm open to other genres.

Something like:

* The Martian
* Project Hail Mary
* Interstellar ("It's impossible." "No, it's necessary.")
* All the planning scenes in Apollo 13, ESPECIALLY Apollo 13
* Tremors
* The 1st half of Oppenheimer

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Have you seen Contact and Contagion?  Not quite the same but still pretty smart. 
  - Contagion is absolutely competence porn. 
2. Master and Commander. Boat competence. 
3. The Big Short
4. Sci fi, competence, but slightly different from your examples: Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home

Edit: most of original and nineties Star Trek heavily feature the most competent characters in the galaxy solving seemingly impossible problems
5. Sneakers
6. My Cousin Vinny

## 2. Need Movies with absolutely Unimaginable mesmerizing soundtracks

**Score:** 41
**Body:** Need movies with beautiful, mesmerizing and unprocessable soundtracks. Scenes where the soundtrack lifts you so much it hits you hard and the scene just becomes a part of you. Examples:- Can you hear the music in Oppenheimer, Time in Inception, Arrival ending scene, and the most probable im looking for is Mr Robots ending episode soundtrack type scenes.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Last of the Mohicans
2. Interstellar  
Annihilation   
It Follows 
3. I recently watched "The Fountain".. It's soundtrack was heavenly. 

Other than that, The Last Kingdom (Series) soundtrack was also outstanding. 
4. Sunshine. John Murphy composed an amazing soundtrack.
5. Tron: Legacy 
6. Drive’s soundtrack is phenomenal not just in the music itself but how it gels together with the film
7. Chariots of Fire
8. Requiem for a Dream and it main theme Lux Aeterna by Clint Mansell 
9. Oblivion with Tom Cruise has such a good score. My friend’s dvd had a sound option where you could play the movie with just the score for the audio track. 
10. Lord of the Rings Trilogy. Shout out Canadian composer Howard Shore for this incredible music! 

## 3. What is a movie that permanently changed how you look at a completely normal, everyday activity?

**Score:** 40
**Body:** Like how The Truman Show makes you look at mirrors differently, or Final Destination ruined driving behind logging trucks for an entire generation. What movie rewired your brain regarding something completely mundane?

### Top 9 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. In The Matrix, 1999 was described as the peak of human civilization, and I laughed, thinking that wouldn’t age well. But then the next 24 years happened, and now I’m like... yeah, okay, maybe the machines had a point.
  - Yeah I loved that the John Wick sequels played homage to iconic Matrix scenes. Proving once again the 90's really was peak.
2. American Beauty helped me realize everyone is not what they seem in public
  - And to enjoy trash dancing in the wind.
3. Every volleyball is now Wilson from Castaway.. 
4. jaws- going in the ocean
5. I never really thought about how much paperwork would be required by police officers in shooting situations until after I saw Hot Fuzz (one of my top ten favorite movies). Apparently Simon Pegg and Nick Frost asked real cops what they’d never seen dramatized in pop culture and they all said ‘the paperwork’. 

Also, I couldn’t stand to be around a tv with a snowy screen after I saw The Ring. 
6. Office Space and going to work. You don’t need to stress about your job. It’s ok to leave it at work. 
7. Fight Club - soap. 
8. How's Your News? It's a documentary/ road trip movie starring a group of uh...developmentally delayed adults, some non-verbal. It showed me  that even a simple interaction, like saying hello, can make their day.  There's a scene with a non verbal guy with CP in a wheelchair, a microphone, and a sign with " talk to me" written on it, parked on a busy street corner.  He is ignored, over and over, as if he is invisible. People walk right past him. Finally, one guy stops, and asks him how he's doing.  The dude in the wheelchair is overcome with joy. He can't talk, but he can make sounds.  The guy on the street can't understand him, of course, but he talks with him, responds to him, as if he's having a real conversation. It's such a beautiful moment in the movie and made me realize how just being seen and treated normally feels to these folks that are typically marginalized.  


## 4. A movie about loneliness that doesn't end with the protagonist finding love.

**Score:** 31
**Body:** Loneliness is a common theme in countless movies, from Deadpool to Adam Sandler movies. Usually the issue of loneliness is resolved by the protagonist by finding love or a partner and it is portrayed as the ultimate resolution of the problem.

Im looking for a movie that focuses more on either self reflection geared towards loneliness or dealing with it in another way. A movie exploring the topic without taking the naturalization that romance is the only way to cope with live in the long run for granted.

Im open to pretty much anything thoughtful even if it contains violence, nudity or mental illness.

3. Her (2013)

5. Shame
6. The Remains of the Day

8. Some Wim Wenders might fit the bill
9. Moon
10. The Wild Pear Tree

The Story of Asya Klyachina, Who Loved, But Did Not Marry

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Christopher Nolan, in a new fascinating interview, discussed the difference between amateur & professional film criticism

**Score:** 604
**Body:** [https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wa4I8Ch2TRo](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wa4I8Ch2TRo)

Nolan described a difference between what amateur film criticism and professional film criticism looks like, and I think had some really interesting points to say on that front which this community might be interested in.

A summary of the quotes (I would really recommend watching the whole video in the link, it is a really fascinating and in-depth interview where he goes into the philosophy of not just 'The Odyssey', but his entire filmography - not a lot of these kind of interviews for movies nowadays):

"The interesting thing about film, and this is, you know, when I was talking about film criticism I was talking more about amateur film criticism than professional film criticism because professional film criticism tends to understand the necessity for the "mechanisms". So you're looking at a lingua franca of storytelling created by Hollywood for the last 100 years that is very effectively universal and so it is its own language. And that language is understood by people all over the world, which is what's incredible about it. And it is a very accessible, modern language of storytelling and it has certain rules. It has conventions - you can break those conventions, you can bend them, you can move them. But you have to be aware of them the whole time.

"Therein is a fundamental flaw of film criticism in a way, or storytelling criticism, because to be able to identify the mechanism does not invalidate the mechanism. And that's a real problem in criticism today, because people have this idea that because I can understand why the story affects me, therefore it didn't work. That's not how storytelling works. Which again, when I mentioned film criticism, I was talking more about amateur film criticism than professional film criticism... because they feel they've identified the mechanism, they feel that it invalidates it. That could be true of certain elements, and film language evolves with that... but we do as filmmakers avail ourselves of that common language. We build on that understanding of "our audience has seen many films." And they understand that language. So, you're playing with that language. It's the language of genre. It's the language of audience sympathy. It's the language of clarity and of narrative direction and how you guide people through a story."

"You can't completely have a tabula rasa... you can't throw everything away. You have to make your choices in terms of how am I orienting the story. So for example, one of my first films, Memento, was a story that I structured in reverse chronologically. But what I retained was a very very clear and simple three-act structure. So the structure of the film, as it's received by the audience, is very, very conventional. But the chronology is unconventional. And so those are the choices you make. That's one example where you say, "Okay, I need this to be extremely familiar underneath so that I can change what's on the surface." And that's a continual mechanism that's evolving and that you're working with the whole time."

### Top 4 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I think what's he's arguing is that amateurs and fans tend to pay more attention to outputs and film practitioners and good professional critiques have an awareness and appreciation of the machine. He seems to be insinuating that with amateur critique, awareness of the machine is somehow invalidating. That if you intuit the three-act structure underneath the movie that it somehow makes the movie worse.

And he's right that is an amateur point of view. It's no different than with music. An amateur might know enough about music to intuit there's a pre-chorus, chorus, bridge, chorus type structure to the song and conclude the song was formulaic. But a professional isn't looking at it this way. The professional accepts that structure as a precondition for pop music and instead asks "did the artist do anything clever with the structure? Did they change key in the second refrain? Was there an interesting turnaround? Did the chord progression change?" It's a much more sophisticated reading. That I can recognize the ii-V-I doesn't invalidate the song, it makes a musician listen harder to see if the artist is going to do something interesting with it. I can recognize the midpoint transition in a movie like Gone Girl and also recognize that it's absolutely brilliant. Or that the T-Rex attack scene in Jurassic Park is a midpoint transition structurally that's exhibited with an amazing virtuosity by Spielberg. Where a lot of amateur criticism gets stuck is that it knows it enough to recognize that the Superman or Indiana Jones themes are a march, for example, and then invalidates it because of the recognition ("this is just a march!"). But what they miss is the sophistication of using a march, a military organizational tool and changing its meaning to represent courage and valor and civic heroics (Superman isn't a military hero and the Olympics aren't about military conquest), which is highly sophisticated re-purposing. That's what makes John Williams so good, but that requires another level of discernment to pick up on. 

A lot of amateur criticism gets caught up on things like plot contrivances or discontinuity as evidence of whether a movie is good or not. Its a bit like saying a Quarterback is bad because he threw three interceptions without realizing the interceptions were caused by a defense disguising it's coverages and confusing him. There's multiple layers to read a product and practitioners and informed critics will tend to read on a different level and worse, the masses will often interpret this as gatekeeping. 

I think what Nolan is sort of warning against is something written about In The London List recently: if you adhere too much to the mass critical zeitgeist it actually isn't democratizing. What it really does is flattens taste into homogenous ubiquity. The YouTube and Twitter critical establishment due to social media's sheer scale ultimately becomes a kind of tastemaker that pushes toward noisy blandness. And the social media landscape only amplifies anti-artistic commercial pathologies that have always been in tension, i.e. the tendency toward loudness, simplicity and easy recognizability (Instagrammable, and Tik Tok-able). 

Fran Lebowitz said something interesting on this:

>"Everyone talked about the effect that AIDS had on the culture ... they talked about what artists were lost, but they never talked about this audience that was lost. ... There was such a high level of connoisseurship ... that made the culture better. A very discerning audience, an audience with a high level of connoisseurship, is exactly as important to the culture as artists. Now, we don't have any kind of discernment. When that audience died ... it allowed the second, third and fourth tier to rise to the front. ... Everything has to be broader, more blatant, more on the nose, because obviously they’re not going to pick up little subtleties. ... It just got dumbed down.” 

  
What modern media critique lacks is a highly discerning audience and what Nolan seems to be saying, at least my read is that the consumer audience and amateur critical world can view connoisseurship itself as the problem or elitist, when high discernment is exactly the thing that gives artists vitality. Rotten Tomatoes treats both as if they were the same thing. A highly informed critique made by someone who knows what they're talking about gets blended with someone running their mouths about nonsense from an obscure blog. 
  - Incredible post. I hope everyone reads it. 

And a tangental side note to add, on the dumbing down of things, we also have this recent phenomenon of things like “Emily In Paris” which allows gaps in the narrative so people can look at their phones while watching, or like Matt Damon said in that interview: the streaming channels ask for the characters to say out loud what is happening in the story multiple times for the audience on their phones. I imagine the peanut galleries of vaudeville where audiences are too busy getting drunk or messing around with their friends to catch every word of the performance and constantly asking each other “eh? What did he say?” so the kind of story took on a certain form to cater for that, and now we see it in film (and related media) but for competition with smart phones. It’s also interesting to note modern amateur reviews left on Amazon of more artistic movies or especially kids novels from the Victorian/Edwardian periods, where there are many 1 star reviews simply because the person watching “couldn’t understand it”, or they say something like “Treasure Island” or “Alice In Wonderland”’cannot be kids books because they are too difficult to read. What was considered a book for children 100 years ago is now considered by some to be too difficult for modern adults.

What is really interesting is that amateur criticism on You Tube and Tiktok has developed it’s own language of reaction shots, editing techniques, delivery styles, and we have so many armchair critics influencing each other to create in specific styles in an attempt to bump up viewers. We have this amazing medium  
which allows everyone to create their own voice, and yet the majority copy the same handful of tricks over and over. 

And then some of these creators graduate to jobs working for “professional” media networks which brings down the overall quality of criticism from institutions that were previously considered pro. I’m thinking of The Guardian for example, and especially their now infamous recent review of the new Boards Of Canada album, which it boggles the mind could make it past any kind of professional editorship.
  - I think it’s an elegant and thoughtful response to the abysmal level of discourse surrounding the odyssey. I don’t think the movie is beyond criticism, but the debate, whether from the self-proclaimed gourmet or anti-mainstream cinephiles, or from the pure rage-bait culture warriors, reached a rare low in terms of online discussion. Very little of it felt genuinely interested in engaging with the film itself.
2. I'm sure what he describes is a real thing but I'm not sure it's the most prominent problem with amateur film criticism. I suppose it depends what he means by amateur film criticism but most of the "reviews" I see on Reddit/YouTube are blighted by other issues - obsession with plot holes, excessive moralising, confusing unlikeable characters with bad writing, misunderstanding of objectivity, etc.
  - I do think that it is a sizable problem with some people, though. It's almost like a response to the trope-heavy storytelling of genre fiction, be it the twisty end of a thriller or the 2nd act break-up of a rom com. People notice that a flash back uses different colour grading and are almost disappointed with this shorthand - or see a "death flag" and are immediately accusing a story of clichéd, bad story telling. Having a character's death foreshadowed in a way similar to other films should not automatically be a reason to invalidate its eventual impact. As an example.
    - Recently saw a comment on Reddit about how in The Dark Knight they manage to save the Social Contract because the people on the ferries make the correct choice in deciding not to blow each other up. 

It was criticized as "bad writing" because in the next movie the people actually do get manipulated into a violent uprising.

For some reason they couldn't understand that the *whole point* of a sequel is escalation! 

In the first movie society (just barely) avoids breaking down. In the sequel society breaks down.

The internet has *always* been a place for bad takes, but it's been particularly bad the last ten or so years. People act like they've never seen a movie or show before.

Nolan actually put it into words in this interview. People think because they've *identified* the short hand that makes it "bad".

But that's just the language of cinema. It's a language we all know from having watched a lifetime of film and tv. You can change it and mess with it, but that has to come from a perspective of still knowing the language for it to work.
  - I'm not sure if this comes under excessive moralising, but I really hate how the consensus at the moment seems to be moving towards "depicting a thing is validating a thing". It's just weird.

Takes I've seen people say *today* include "Obsession validates sexual assault" and "This Ends With Us validates abusive relationships". In both films, abusive and sexual assault (and rape for Obsession) take place, in neither film is it shown as a positive thing. 

People get really confused when the antagonist is a main character. 
    - I’ve been noticing this more and more in personal reviews on social media and Letterboxd, and it really does seem to be becoming a popular - or at least increasingly vocal - way of interacting with media. I’m sure it’s tied to diminishing media literacy. There aren’t really words strong enough to express how much I hate this idea that “depicting is validating”.   

This morning I watched *On the Count of Three” and then read through Letterboxd reviews  - and there was more than one that basically amounted to “this movie is sick for saying that >!molestation victims should kill themselves!<”. It seems like every time I read/listen to reviews lately, these kind of reductive and frankly brainrotted takes pop up a lot. It makes me wish there was an easy way to get into arguments on Letterboxd.
  - There’s a reason experimental and art house films usually aren’t very popular. Threading that needle is almost impossible, and ultimately if you want to keep working, you need to sell tickets. 
3. “Because they feel they’ve identified the mechanism, they feel that it invalidates it”

I’ve certainly seen examples of this - people talking dismissively of tropes and other storytelling mechanisms as soon as they spot them as if their mere presence is a gotcha moment for the film and the filmmaker. 

On the other hand, movies are getting obnoxiously formulaic (the success of entire franchises was built on this), and that’s even before getting into the “are they or are they not writing movies for people who watch on their phones while multitasking” debate. So sometimes spotting a worn trope is imo used as a shortcut for identifying this kind “low effort” production/artistic value, which may or may not be accurate depending on the case ofc. 

And even once we all accept the premise (that there is a common language for filmmaking - and critiquing - with its own rules), there’s plenty of room left for debating whether those universal tools have been used effectively or not to “guide people through a story”, which is a beautiful way for Nolan to put what making a movie is about for him, I think. 

## 2. which directors have the clearest philosophy behind their films?

**Score:** 93
**Body:** &#x200B;

I'm not necessarily talking about directors who directly reference philosophers or make obviously philosophical movies.

I mean filmmakers whose movies seem to return to the same underlying beliefs aboiut human nature, morality, existence...

The kind where, after watching a few of their films, you start to feel like you know how they see the world.

A clear one is Haneke's and his deep pessimism about modern society,  or Ozu who seems to approach life with such a quiet acceptance that resides in his characters.

However, kubrick is fascinating to me because almost every film seems to question whether humans are capable of overcoming their own instincts. Whether it's violence and war (fullmetal jacket), ambition and social acceptance (eyes wide shut)... ALWAYS with that component of altered sexuality (far beyond those in which it is the key theme, like in Lolita) which is the main thing I focused on when I recently rewatched all his entire career. Watch the subliminal references to sexuality in Dr strangelove, fr. Things I read in some books about Kubrick, not that I figured out myself tbh hahahah. 

But this man's morality feels sometimes so ambiguous that I never get to fully catch his philosophy as clear as others. That complexity is something I love, don't missunderestand me.

Forgive me if I did misspelled something, spanish member here ✌️

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. The Coen Brothers have an existential absurdist viewpoint throughout much of their work. A Serious Man is probably the best example.

Their adaptation of No Country worked so well in part because their absurdist existentialism is well suited to McCarthy's pessimism.

4. Funnily enough, when I read the title of your post, Kubrick was the first director that came to my mind. However complicated or obtuse his philosophy may appear, it can't be denied it's there and that Kubrick invites us to figure it out. 

As you rightly point out, Kubrick is interested in human nature, and whether it's possible for humans to transcend it. The most literal example of this is, of course, 2001, where alien intervention allows humanity to evolve beyond the human condition. But without the help of aliens, elsewhere in Kubrick humans fail to make this transition, usually resulting in catastrophe. 

Kubrick's films always deal with what I think of as the Kubrickian paradox (it may be Kubrick was influenced by philosophy and his paradox is taken from some famous philosopher I don't know about - excuse my lack of education there [but if that's the case, it's probably Nietzsche]). The paradox is that the qualities that allowed humans to evolve into such a spectacularly successful species (and for Kubrick this evolution is no less than a miracle) are the very same qualities that prevent humans from evolving any further. Our genius is one and the same with our downfall. 

For Kubrick, the genius is inextricably linked to aggression, and our instinct to exert dominance over others. Again, 2001 is the clearest example. In that film, the thing that marks the birth of humanity is the invention of the first weapon. And it's the quest for domination that leads to the amazing technical advancement humans have achieved. 

But as the technology advances further and further, it becomes further and further detached from humans themselves - from our bodies, our limbs, our own physical energy and vitality. In time, it deadens us, makes us flat, inactive; 'dull boys'. Kubrick links this phenomenon to the advancement of capital, to the marketisation of every aspect of human life, so that even our most intimate communications with loved ones get monetised, allocated a market value. 

Never one to keep things simple, Kubrick gives all of this an extra level by contextualising it in terms of gender. The aggressive driving force of humanity is identified as masculine, patriarchal. Its opposing force, that which seeks to pacify man and to render him ineffectual (or 'safe'), is classified as feminine, matriarchal. This is where Kubrick's reputation as a misogynist comes from, and honestly it's difficult to deny the accusation. Kubrick, a man with a wife and three daughters, made films that were unapologetically misogynist. 

As for morality, I don't think Kubrick is concerned with it. Perhaps morality, in the Kubrick universe, is what morality was for Nietzsche; a symptom of human failing, of the resentment of the weak towards the powerful. 

None of this is to say Kubrick was some kind of master race fantasist. He wasn't. Ultimately, I don't think his films suggest any solution to the paradox that preoccupied him (apart from that one time with the aliens, of course). He recognised that, historically speaking, those who have sought a solution have been responsible for the most terrible human suffering. I think he simply presents us with a truth he perceives within that unsolvable paradox. He shows it to us over and over, saying 'Look - this is what humans are. This is why we're amazing, and this is also why we're terrible'. His reaction is either to laugh or to be horrified, and he seeks to share both his laughter and his horror with the world.
  - I never found Kubrick's filmography to be especially misogynistic, at least by the standards of his time. Depictions of women in a Hitchcock, De Palma or Scorsese film are infinitely more problematic. It's just that war, juvenile delinquency, slave revolts and Cold War war rooms are predominantly male pastimes. The absence of women and their appearance at the end of Paths of Glory and Full Metal Jacket could be as you said, a counterpoint to the toxic masculine energy, but Lolita and Eyes Wide Shut feature more nuanced and complex portrayals. There is a general misanthropic quality in Kubrick's work, but it never felt malicious towards women.

## 3. Satoshi Kon, Darren Aronofsky, and AI

**Score:** 74
**Body:** In a [documentary made after Kon's death](https://letterboxd.com/film/satoshi-kon-the-illusionist/), Darren Aronofsky recalls the famous bathtub scene in *Requiem for a Dream*. He explains that he was searching for a way to externalize Jennifer Connelly's psychological state when he happened to watch *Perfect Blue*. Struck by one particular sequence, he wrote to Kon asking whether he would mind if it were recreated as a homage. Kon generously agreed. Aronofsky later recalled meeting him in Japan, where Kon supposedly told him he was proud of the tribute and genuinely delighted by it.

Years later, however, [an older interview](https://youtu.be/63btRwOWbUA?si=v23b1i7bx7l4xydW) with Kon resurfaced on anime forums and Reddit after Aronofsky's AI project drew renewed attention to his relationship with Kon's work. In the interview, Kon himself plays the two films side by side, pointing out the nearly identical angles, compositions, and staging. When he asked Aronofsky about the similarities, the answer was simple:

"It's a homage."

Kon laughs as he points to himself with a stick.

"*A homage... to me.*"

Everyone in the room laughs with him. Then the joke fades. Kon remarks that Aronofsky had essentially treated *Perfect Blue* as a ready-made storyboard. The interviewer tries to soften the exchange by saying that there are certainly many similarities. Kon responds with a question that lingers much longer than the laughter:

*"Similarities... or theft?"*

In the same interview, almost as comic relief, Kon mentions that he happened to be on the same flight as Jennifer Connelly. She was flying first class with her family, while he was sitting in business class.

Kon died of pancreatic cancer in 2010 at only 46 years old, before receiving the worldwide recognition he deserved. Then came *Black Swan*. This time the parallels were even harder to ignore, yet Aronofsky denied that the film was influenced by Kon, describing it simply as a dramatization of *Swan Lake*. By then, Kon was no longer around to respond.

Adding another layer to the story, [Perfect Blue's producer later revealed](https://www.dazeddigital.com/film-tv/article/37923/1/darren-aronofsky-wanted-to-remake-perfect-blue) that Aronofsky had previously tried to acquire the live-action rights to the film before eventually making *Black Swan*.

None of this is new, but it came back to my mind when I remembered the ended wave of AI-generated "Ghiblification."

What surprised me wasn't that AI could imitate Studio Ghibli's visual language. It was learning that Japan allows AI models to be trained on copyrighted works, despite having some of the world's strictest copyright laws and one of the narrowest approaches to fair use.

But maybe the legal question isn't even the most interesting one.

Can an artistic style actually belong to someone?

Can Ghibli's watercolor palettes, dreamlike atmosphere, visual rhythm, and decades of accumulated craftsmanship be considered intellectual property? Should style itself be protected from being compressed into a prompt—not just individual frames or drawings, but the artistic language that gives them meaning?

I don't know.

## 4. Fail Safe (1964): the serious nuclear-war film that came out the same year as Dr. Strangelove and got buried. It's the one that actually scared me.

**Score:** 64
**Body:** I finally watched Fail Safe last week and I'm a little annoyed nobody made me see it sooner.

It's the serious version of Dr. Strangelove. Same year, same studio, basically the same premise. A technical fault sends a group of American bombers past the point of no return with orders to nuke Moscow, and nobody can call them back. Strangelove made that funny. Sidney Lumet made it a nightmare.

The thing that got me first is that there's no music in the entire film. No score at all. I didn't even notice for a while, I just felt increasingly tense and couldn't figure out why. Turns out it's because Lumet took away the thing every thriller uses to tell you when to be scared, and honestly that quiet is more stressful than any score would've been. You're just sitting in these rooms with these people.

What really separates it from Strangelove is where it puts the blame. Strangelove says the problem is people, specifically deranged, paranoid, weird people. Fail Safe says the problem is the system. Every single character is competent and sane and doing their job correctly, and it still nearly ends the world. There's no lunatic to stop. That messed with me more than any villain would have.

Also, Walter Matthau is in it, cast completely against type as a coldblooded academic who argues that a first strike killing tens of millions is basically fine if the math works out. He's so calm about it.

Most of Henry Fonda's screen time is just him in a bare room with a translator, on the phone with the Soviet premier. It shouldn't be tense and it's unbearable, especially the pauses while the translator works.

Anyone else seen this? Curious how other people took the ending, as a tragedy or as the only rational move left.
